utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 2nd of March, 2010. I would like, first of all, to greet General Petkovic, who's here in the courtroom, all the accused in the courtroom, Defence counsel, the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us. I shall, first of all, hand down two oral decisions. First oral decision pertaining to the Petkovic Defence application for extra time for the additional examination of Milivoj Petkovic. On the 24th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence filed a public request with a view to asking the Chamber to grant it, overall, 15 minutes for its additional examination of Milivoj Petkovic after the questions put by the Judges. As a preliminary matter, the Trial Chamber would like to recall that in its oral decision of the 23rd of February, 2010, it stipulated that the Petkovic Defence would be entitled to address those topics that had been addressed by the Judges as part of the questions put to Milivoj Petkovic during the additional examination or re-examination. The Trial Chamber had thus dismissed the possibility of a new examination-in-chief after the questions of the Judges. The Trial Chamber notes, moreover, that the Petkovic Defence has exhausted the time credit allocated by the Trial Chamber, pursuant to guide-line number 5, to conduct its examination-in-chief and its re-examination. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides to grant 15 extra minutes to the Petkovic Defence to enable it to conduct its re-examination, which will take place after the cross-examination of the Prosecution. Second oral decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting the Chamber, but I'd ask the Registry to please pass on that I would like to address the Chamber -- I'd like to address the Chamber prior to the Chamber ruling on this matter. As the Chamber knows, the Petkovic Defence filed a response yesterday afternoon, and I believe the Coric filed a paper joining in that submission, Your Honours. First of all, I should say good morning to all of Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to counsel, all those in the courtroom. Your Honour, I do feel -- and I would ask leave before the Chamber rules, to make a short oral reply about this matter, because I think it's of the utmost importance. Of course, I don't know what the Chamber's inclination or anticipated ruling is, but nevertheless, Your Honour, if the Chamber will allow me one minute -- two minutes. Your Honour, the simple truth of the matter is this, in response to the submissions made: Under any honest assessment -- under any honest assessment, Mr. Petkovic, at least for all of the co-accused, perhaps putting Mr. Coric's counsel to one side we have yet to see, so I don't pre-judge that, but as to all the Defence questioning to date, there is no way that that can be considered to be cross-examination. What we have seen here, and this has been an ongoing issue in the case as the Chamber knows is this has been for all practical purposes by any realistic, genuine, authentic measure, a common witness used by each of the co-accused to advance their own case, to conduct their own further examinations, all in the nature or substantially in the nature of direct examination. If the proper label was applied, we might call it "truth in labelling." I know food and drugs have to have truthful information on the packaging. If we had truthful labelling about this, these would be nothing more than direct examinations, in which case there would be no mystery about the Prosecution's full opportunity to respond to all the direct examinations with adequate time, applying the Chamber's usual rules. It is the complete elevation of form over substance, for fairness to the Prosecution to be determined what a label being applied, if this is supposedly something called cross-examination, when it is not and has not been. To consider the situation further, Your Honours, there's only one part in the courtroom -- party, there's only one party in the courtroom who's going to challenge and test Mr. Petkovic's evidence, again, leaving to one side Mr. Coric's counsel, which again I won't pre-judge. But there's only one party, and that's the Prosecution, it is genuinely going to test and challenge this witness's evidence. We need sufficient time to do that. We are trying to assist the Chamber, and we hope the Chamber will take that sincerely. We are trying to address a number of issues. There's a huge number of issues to be addressed, and the Prosecution needs adequate time and a fair amount of time in order to address all the issues that have been raised. And, of course, there was the lengthy examination by the President. Mr. President, I have never said and I don't think anyone in the courtroom has ever said that we question your right or opportunity to do that. That is not my point at all. I appreciate the Court's questioning. I think it's often helpful, and I appreciate that. There's no question about that. But the reality remains that when there is a lengthy additional examination, questions are raised, topics are raised, new things are said. Mr. Petkovic gives additional answers a different way, different topics, new documents, that require response, that requires for the Prosecution to be able to get its perspective and its challenge to certain parts of the evidence. Therefore, Your Honour, we stand by our request. We think it's a reasonable request under these particular circumstances. In all the time that's been given to the Defence, there's not been a single Defence team that's gotten up so far who has not been granted more time; in fact several more extensions of time, such as Mr. Praljak yesterday, Can I have more time, can I have more time, can I have more time? The Prosecution asks to be treated fairly and given sufficient time to be able to assist the Chamber in covering the important topics that need to be covered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just say we don't understand, the Petkovic Defence, we don't understand why all these issues which Mr. Scott has mentioned in the last few minutes aren't fully covered in the written submissions, the motion that the Prosecution was invited to put in, the response that we put in. So I'm certainly not going to follow Mr. Scott and repeat what we have got there on paper. We do say, with respect, that the last four or five -- well, it's not four or five minutes, however many minutes Mr. Scott's been on his feet, has been a waste of time. That's what those written submissions were for. Your Honours have them and, no doubt, will rule upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, with your leave, I do, with the greatest of respect, and however unwittingly, deprecate the, on occasion, lack of, well, self-indulgence to simply address the Bench on any issue many, many times. It's often the case that submissions do not get better by mere repetition. Now, Your Honours will determine in due course whether or not, for example, the questioning put forward by my lead counsel in relation to this witness was friendly cross-examination, all add item, on all material issues, or whether or not on the substance, no the tone, on the substance if there was a material distinction between the case of Mr. Stojic and that of Mr. Petkovic. The Prosecution can say as many times as they want, until they are exhausted, until the Court is exhausted, that there is one defence here, and they have the truth-seeking role. The Defence will not for a moment cede that ground. The Defence, in our respectful submission, are as much interested and as much engaged in the truth-seeking role as any other party in this courtroom, as well and including my learned friends on the other side. So, Your Honours, I would ask -- I would join the submissions of my learned friend Mr. Stewart that there has been an opportunity to vent these issues in writing. Counsel should not simply take latitude that's given by the Bench to address issues many, many times, because it does, as Judge Prandler said repeatedly, eat into very precious court time. There are many cases in this courtroom and in this building that are wishing to be heard, and we all must be rather disciplined in the time we take on our feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues and ask them whether these submissions modify our decision in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has handed down its decision, and I shall present my personal opinion. Oral decision relating to the Prosecution's application for extra time for the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. On the 26th of February, 2010, the Prosecution filed a public motion in which it requested the Trial Chamber to grant it 13 hours and 36 minutes overall for its cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. In its oral decision of 11th of February, 2010, the Trial Chamber had allocated the Prosecution, for its cross-examination, the same amount of time as that that had been granted to the Petkovic Defence for its examination-in-chief and its re-examination, i.e., six hours. The Petkovic Defence, having had six hours and forty minutes, forty extra minutes have thus been accorded to the Prosecution also. In light of the extra time granted to the Petkovic Defence for its examination-in-chief and its re-examination, and of the extra time accorded to the Defence teams for their respective cross-examinations and the topics addressed when the questions were put to Milivoj Petkovic by the Presiding Judge, the Trial Chamber holds that it should also grant extra time to the Prosecution. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides to grant the Prosecution two hours and twenty minutes for its cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic and notes that the Prosecution now has nine hours overall to cross-examine Milivoj Petkovic. My personal opinion runs as follows: I fully share in the decision that has been taken by the Trial Chamber as regards the possibility that the Prosecution will have to have three extra hours, compared with the initial time that had been granted on the 11th of February, 2010; i.e., six hours. Accordingly, the Prosecution has 50 per cent of extra time. As far as the reasons behind this extra time, as far as I'm concerned, this stems from the questions put by the other Defence teams and not provided by any individual Judge. On close scrutiny of the practices developed in all the other Trial Chambers show that as far as time is concerned and the time used by the Bench, this Bench is included in the overall time allotted to the parties, i.e., Prosecution or Defence. For instance, in the Karadzic case, the Trial Chamber has decided to grant a number of hours to the Prosecution and to the Defence, and in this time are included the housekeeping matters as well as the questions from the Bench, if there are any. In addition, all the other Chambers have adopted the guide-lines, i.e., the decision to grant for cross-examination, whatever it may be, 80 per cent of the time in order to expedite the trial, irrespective of matters of substance raised. As far as possible questions relating to issues not addressed are concerned, I would like to recall that I addressed things two ways; i.e., the indictment was the first part, and the second part was the Defence case. During the first day, my questions only related to the indictment and on P exhibits of the Prosecution, which were known to the Prosecution, as it seemed the Prosecution familiar with its case, of course, cannot indicate that these are new topics. As far as the Defence is concerned, I have only used those exhibits that had been mentioned during examination-in-chief, and I did not address any new topics, with the exception of the question of Prozor following Mr. Scott's intervention. That said, there are the causes and consequences to be addressed. If nine hours are granted, this is only a consequence of a cause. The main cause has to do with the interpretation of Rule 90(H) by the Trial Chamber. This interpretation seems to be contrary to the spirit of the article. Rule 90(H) stipulates that the cross-examination should be limited to. The mere factor that the Rules stipulated that it should be limited to means that those people who drafted the Rules indicated that the cross-examination should be limited. In what way is it limited? It is limited to three questions: issues mentioned during examination-in-chief; issues relating to the credibility of the witness; and issues relating to the case presented by the parties. The main problem is due to the interpretation one makes of a party's case; (ii), Rule 90(H), settles the issue, and this, I think, some people have lost sight of this. Let me stipulate what it means. In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case, for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of that case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence. This word, "contradiction," is the most important term. The person who is cross-examining is going to contradict the topic that has been addressed. That said, I fully agree with what Mr. Scott said a few minutes ago, when he said that the cross-examination is, in fact, an examination-in-chief. In my view, there should be no cross-examination, save for the situation where there are varying opinions between the accused, and in that case the cross-examination is justified. Yesterday, Mr. Praljak attested to this. At no point in time was he in contradiction with General Petkovic. Nonetheless, he was granted one hour and ten minutes. Had he been in contradiction with, then he could have. To conclude, I would like to quote two case laws of the ICTY of February 2004 -- ICTR of 2004. The president was Mrs. Vaz, who is currently an Appeals Chamber Judge, for the people who don't know this. This was in the Andre Rwamakuba case. In paragraph 15 of its decision, let me quote - this is extremely short - it states: "The Trial Chamber holds that the decision does not jeopardise the outcome of the trial in any way." It is noted that in its decision of the 5th of December, 2003, the Chamber only established a framework and a guide-line. During the cross-examination of another witness by the counsel of another accused, the Trial Chamber clarified its decision by maintaining that this was not equality, in arithmetical terms, and that it held that it would decide on a case-by-case basis, i.e., analyse any specific situation. If limits on the time in cross-examination are needed, the Chamber can, nonetheless, accord more time to a party that needs it, only if this does not lead to an unjustified waste of time. The second case law text stems from the judgement by the Appeals Chamber in the Akayesu case. In this well-known case, in paragraph 317, the Presiding Judge had been told that he had controlled the time of the cross-examination. The Appeals Chamber states the intervention by the Presiding Judge had a particular purpose, which was to control the proceedings, and these were aimed at the parties involved in the trial. The Prosecutor and his associates, in paragraph 318, the Appeals Chamber states that the Appeals Chamber holds that the Presiding Judge fulfilled his role, which he is invested with, and may control the time of examination-in-chief and cross-examination-in-chief when witnesses come to testify. I haven't finished. The Appeals Chamber thus recalled that the time allocated for cross-examination is monitored, and the person monitoring such time is the Presiding Judge. I, therefore, feel that time should be granted when there is a need for it. Cross-examination does not amount to examination-in-chief. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'd like to make a request with regard to the decision on the time allocated to the Prosecution for the cross-examination of General Petkovic. But, first of all, I would like to ask you for a little patience and allow me to say a few words. If we carefully analyse the cross-examination of General Petkovic, regardless of whether one considers this examination to be friendly or unfriendly, we will then see that this examination has nothing to do with the questions that Judge Antonetti put to General Petkovic. This story about Judge Antonetti's questions has been blown out of all proportion in this courtroom in order to lay a foundation for a request for additional time and so that the Prosecution can satisfy his desire for additional time. Your Honour, please allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, just 15 seconds. We handed down a decision, so you're not supposed to comment on the decision. You can ask for a certification of appeal, and then we can issue a decision straight away. But if you want the floor in order to say that you agree with me in saying that the Prosecutor should not be granted any additional time because of the questions I put, well, I said I was in favour of that in the decision. Now, as to the time allotted, that stems from the questions put by the other Defence teams, but that's over. So why do you want to take the floor again?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you why. In the course of the break, I would like you to request -- I would like to request you to allow me to have contact with General Petkovic so that we can agree on what we should do with regard to your decision on additional time for Prosecution examination. I don't believe that we just have the possibility of filing an appeal. I think that there is other -- there are other means of appeal, but I'd like to consult General Petkovic about this. But in order to be able to confer with my client in a satisfactory manner, I believe that we ought to know -- could Judge Trechsel please allow me to say this. If the Prosecution gets two hours and twenty minutes on the basis of Judges' questions and on the basis of questions put by other Defence teams, I would like to know exactly how much time is being allocated on the basis of the Judges' questions, and I would like to know which questions are concerned. I would like to know on the basis of which questions from other Defence teams this time is being allocated, and I would like to know whether the Chamber will control the way in which this additional time is being used. It's important for us to have this information so that we can decide as to the steps to take, the legal steps to take, with regard to your decision on additional time for the Prosecution. If you would allow me to have contact with General Petkovic, I will tell you what our position is immediately after having spoken to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break, and you can then consult with General Petkovic. Of course, there's no problem whatsoever. Let's start with the Coric Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to do make one correction, Mr. President, because you indicated that General Praljak did nothing but direct examination, and I just want to give an example because I don't want -- I want to make sure that the Trial Chamber realises what we're trying to do. Yesterday, the general was confronted with certain documents concerning Halilovic. Now, the general's initial opinion was that General Praljak was absolutely wrong about Halilovic, and he held Halilovic, it would appear, in very high esteem, other than the fact that Halilovic couldn't be trusted for his word. Documents were shown. The general admitted that he had not seen those documents, granted there should have been one more question, such as, Now that you see these documents, do you change your opinion? That question wasn't asked. But that being said, now there seems to be evidence before us, at least, giving rise to a different interpretation as to what General Petkovic initially indicated. At some point, it may be relevant, because obviously Halilovic is a big player in this case. This is an example of where we can say that nothing but direct examination was done. I don't want to go into all the specifics, but I do think that sometimes there are useful ways of getting information in through cross-examination, and this was one of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just mention something? On the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll give you the floor in a moment. Yes, Mr. Karnavas, on this very specific example of Halilovic, I agree with you. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At page 9, it was just Your Honour's explanation and views on Rule 90, the need to include what Your Honour said, which is at page 9, line 5. Your Honour was referring to Rule 90(H)(i), and then at page 9, at line 13, Your Honour was referring to Rule 90(H)(ii). Otherwise, the explanation doesn't appear at all clear. Your Honour knows, I think, already that we accept, as we have to, the majority decision of the Trial Chamber, which the Petkovic Defence, with the greatest respect, regards as absolutely right, and Your Honour knows that we do not accept Your Honour's minority view which you've expounded again this morning. But it's already in decisions made, so there's absolutely no question of my re-arguing any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are absolutely right. We were talking about 90(H)(ii), and then it is in relation to 90(H)(i). Thank you for making it clear. I had not noticed it in the transcript. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but again, I mean, Ms. Alaburic I have to address, and I want the opportunity -- I want the Prosecution to have the opportunity to respond when certain issues are raised. Ms. Alaburic put certain propositions before the Chamber. I certainly disagree with it, and if the Chamber is minded to consider it further, other than having contact -- she can have contact with Mr. Petkovic. I don't care, that's fine. But she asked for certain other things in her submissions, and if the Chamber is minded to entertain those at all, then before the Court rules and before the Court forms its decision, I want the Prosecution to be heard on those. So I would ask the Chamber to advise me and give me the opportunity to address any additional matters raised by the Petkovic Defence prior to the Chamber ruling on them, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the Coric Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would like to say that I have handed out three binders to make it easier to follow my cross-examination. The first binder has some Post-its in it, and it contains certain documents I will be showing Mr. Petkovic. They have been organised in the order that I will be showing them to Mr. Petkovic in. I will also refer to Mr. Petkovic's testimony in the Blaskic and Kordic cases, and I'll show him certain transcript pages which are contained in the main binder, which also has Post-its. There are two other binders, just in case. These are the full transcripts from the Blaskic and Kordic case, so everyone in the courtroom can check these transcript pages that are in the main binder and check to see that they correspond to the actual transcripts. I don't want there to be any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, when answering a question put to you by your counsel - it's on page 49408 of the transcript - you said that the chief of the Main Staff wasn't involved in taking decisions that concerned the organisation and the responsibility of the military police. Could you please have a look at the first document in the binder, P00960. This is a document dated the 28th of December, 1992. They are the instructions on organising the units of the military police. On the first page in the Croatian version, the third paragraph from the bottom - its page 2 in the English version somewhere in the middle - it says: "When manning military police units, the active military police units, the committees in the operative zones have to ensure that there is territorial representation in municipalities which is in proportion to the population of each municipality." We'll skip the next two paragraphs, and then it says: "For the purpose of reorganising the VP units, we propose that commissions consisting of the following members be established:" A, for the first active-service battalion, we can see that a representative of the Main Staff of the HVO is proposed as chairman. And then under B, it says, for battalions in the OZ, we have a proposal for one member of the commission, a battalion commander -- an operative zone commander. Correction. And then we go further down. In English, it's page 4, paragraph 2, and it says: "Officers and commanders will be appointed in accordance with the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department after the 10th of January, 1993, by which time the commissions from each OZ must send a list of proposed candidates for commanding and officer posts in the OZ. In making this proposal, co-operate with all brigade commanders in the OZ and the HVO of the municipality from which a certain candidate is being proposed." It's been signed by the head of the Defence Department. Mr. Petkovic, tell me -- I have just one question: Were you familiar with this, what I have just read out from the document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This is the first time I have seen this document, and I would like to see the list of the members of commission under A and B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Petkovic. I just wanted to know whether you were familiar with this. You said you weren't. That's fine. Let's move on to the next subject. In response to a question put to you by Judge Antonetti, according to which there were two types of military police, one of which was attached to brigades, and this is page 49791 of the transcript, in response to that question you said that as far as you were concerned, there was only one military police, not two, but some of them were responsible for carrying out duties within brigades. Mr. Petkovic, let us now look at what you said about this same topic in the Kordic case. We'll be looking at page 26776, lines 9 through 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, when you mention figures, do read them slowly, because it's not easy for interpreters. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The document number -- or, rather, the transcript reference is P10029. I see that the pages have been correctly recorded, so now I'm reading from the page I mentioned and the following page, and that is 26777, line 1. I'll be reading in English. The interpreters have the very same pages in front of them, and it says [In English]: "Q. I'm moving strictly in chronological order. We gave military police -- commanders of brigades, when they were formed, had military police units attached to them, did they not, General? "A. Yes, yes. "Q. Those units were, from the inception of the brigades, under the control of their brigade commanders; correct? "A. Yes. "Q. Thank you. "A. In the order, it says that the brigade military police was under the command of the brigade commanders. "Q. Yes. This document, indeed you've read it already, as it's been before you, dated the 17th of August, describes the present position. It doesn't describe a change. It's simply describing the position that had always been in effect since the brigades and brigade military police came into being . "A. Yes, Your Honour."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, do you remember saying this in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I -- you said Blaskic now. Didn't you say Kordic before?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, this is obviously my statement in the Kordic case, but it is not in contradiction with the statement that I gave to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, you don't need to interpret. The question was straightforward. So you said it. Now let us look at -- I will remind everybody in the courtroom, because we listened to this all together - it can't be found in the binder - I'll remind you of the words of Mr. Tokic, Witness, in this case, and it was recorded on transcript page 45507, lines 14 through 18. Before I read it out, let me remind everybody that Mr. Tokic was a Defence witness of General Praljak's, and he was a commander of a brigade from Gornji Vakuf; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic says the following: [In English] "Sir, apart from the Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf-Uskopje, there was also, well, the battalion -- well, it was called the battalion, but it had up to 60 men from the Bruno Busic Regiment and then the military police, and then there was a platoon-size units from HOS, the brigade police, which was under my composition. They were units which had the mobilisation establishment and schedule and was made up of men from Gornji Vakuf." Mr. Petkovic, do you remember this part of Mr. Tokic's testimony? You were in the courtroom then.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tokic testified about the structure of the military police. He had military police in his brigade, and that is not a matter of contention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. I would like to ask you a technical question now. When we say "establishment structure," is that the number of organisational units of a military unit or organisation? When we say that something is in the establishment of something else, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it will be part of that brigade and act within that brigade. There is no doubt that the platoon of military police acted within the brigade, but it was also part of the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Petkovic. You don't have to explain things. Just answer my question. Now let's see P04262. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: There is no English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that this was forwarded to all OZs, and we can also see that it was received by all brigades. I can see that it hasn't been recorded that this is your warning. As we have read it several times in this courtroom, I will not show everything. Let us start with the heading: "I hereby warn," and let us read the first item. It says: "The brigade military police is directly subordinate to the brigade commanders. It is also part of the brigade establishment and has the same status as other units within the brigade." Now, I would like to ask you to look at another document in connection with this first item, and that's document P01099. The document is called "Schematic Illustration of the Establishment of the Brigade." Let us look at page 2, where there is the first schematic. We can see that third from the left there's also a platoon of the military police. Mr. Petkovic, do you agree that this schematic we've just seen confirms what you say in item 1 of document P04262 which I've read out a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It does confirm that there was a platoon of military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, all right, Mr. Petkovic, just yes or no. Let's be brief, because my time is extremely limited. Let us look at item 2 of document P04262, the selection of -- or, rather, recruiting manpower to be carried out only from the military structure of a brigade, and the commander has a right to replace every military policeman. Let us now look at document P0 -- PD05106 -- PD05106. 5D, sorry, not PD. 5D. 5D05106. This is a document a document signed by the Frankopan Brigade commander. It's dated the 3rd of April, 1993. And he says: "Pursuant to an order issued by the commander of the OZ and the authorisation of the brigade commander, the Command of the Frankopan Brigade appoints" so-and-so" to the post of the platoon commander of the brigade military police." Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, does this document illustrate the practical implementation of what we have read under item 2 of your warning?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, because the brigade commander has no right to appoint the commander of a platoon of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petkovic, I'm not sure about that, because we saw what this says. But, anyway, the brigade commander appointed the platoon commander, and this is an exhibit already. This refers to Central Bosnia, and it shows that one commander was replaced by another. Stanko Primorac, Cane, was in the Ljubuski Brigade. We don't need to show the document because it's an exhibit already. P00990, that's the document number, the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I must reply to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't. You said that he had no right to do so, and I don't want to go into that. I'm merely showing the fact that an appointment was made. Let us move on to item 4 of our document, which says: "All problems within the brigade police are your problems and should be tackled via the system of command." Let us now look at document 5D05107, which has to do with that. This is an order by brigade commander or the commander of the Vitez Brigade, dated the 22nd of March, 1993, in which he says: "Pursuant to the provisions of the Rule Book on Military Discipline, I order: "Brigade policemen Ivica Rajic and Ivica Jukic fail to carry out orders and behaved carelessly and behaved non-militarily, and thus are subject to the provisions of the Rule Book on Military Discipline, and 15 per cent shall be deducted from their monthly salaries." Under item 2, we see that it says the amount deducted from their salaries shall be given to those policemen who prove best. Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, is the brigade commander here tackling a problem in the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is illegal. He had no right to do that. Only the Disciplinary Court was entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- that was not my question. My question was whether or not he actually did so. Let us look at another document, P02595. Again, the commander of the Vitez Brigade, but this time on the 1st of June, 1993, again based on the Rule Book on Military Discipline, orders Dragan Calic, a member of the Vitez Brigade, and the brigade police, violated the disciplinary rules and is redeployed from the Vitez Brigade to the line of defence. Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, does the brigade commander here, too, deal with an issue within the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, redeploying somebody to the line of defence is not a military -- is not a disciplinary measure. Whoever wrote this didn't have a clue. But, of course, nobody can prevent the brigade commander from sending somebody to the line of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Petkovic, all right. Let's move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, before you answer the question, take some time, because the interpreters are telling me that there's a lot of overlapping and they're getting a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will act in accordance. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to the following topic. On page 49793 of the transcript, you said that there were four so-called standard battalions of the military police which performed duties of the military police. Did you mean the four battalions that were ones in the zones of operation, one each?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one battalion per OZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at what you said about that in the Blaskic case. The document number is P10028, and the page of the transcript that I'll be reading is in the binder with the tabs. I'll read -- I'll start reading with page 24015, lines 1 through 5: [In English] "There were battalions of the military police in every military district or, rather, in the every area covered by military district, there was a certain battalion of the military police." [Interpretation] Now on the very same page, let's have a look at line 15: [In English] "The rules on the establishment and work of the military police stipulates as follows: "1. That all units of the military police are subordinated to the chief of Administration of the Military Police from the point of personnel, organisational, logistics, training and other activities pertaining to the military police. However, the rules stipulate that in carrying out regular military police tasks, the units of the military police shall be subordinate ..." [Interpretation] Now we have certain technical difficulties here, so we will go on to page 24016, and your answer continues at line 10: [In English] "... that in carrying out regular military police tasks, the units of the military police are subordinate to the commander of the operative zone or to another military territorial commander; for the most part, we had commanders of operative zones. "In order to make this clearer, I shall invoke the tasks, the military/territorial tasks, that the military police carries out. The first task of the military police is the protection of lives and the personal safety and security of military personnel. "A brief comment: This task the military police carries out within the area of the operative zone. There is exceptional interest in this task on the part of the commander of the operative zone. It is logical that for carrying out such a task, the military police is responsible to the commander of the operative zone." [Interpretation] We are now on the following page, 2417. I'll very briefly read out passage 3, 7, 12, 20, 23. I'll read out those lines, in fact. And on page 24018, lines 5 to 8, I'll read out the other tasks that you referred to: [In English] "Secondly, discovery of punishable acts. "The next task: Traffic safety. "Furthermore, providing security for safety and military persons. "Furthermore, it supervises the conduct of military personnel, but military personnel who are in the region of that particular operative zone. "Furthermore, it contacts military individuals and accompanies them if they are members of operative zone. There can also be other individuals taking them into custody. "Furthermore, participation in combatting sabotage units ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, tell me -- well, now I'd have to look at -- now I'd like to have a look at the transcript from the Kordic case, page 26820. I'd like to have a look at what you said there. P10029 is the number from the Kordic case. 26820 is the page I'll be reading out, lines 10 to 16: [In English] "Your Honours, yes, there was a continuity of command under the military police, and I believe that in archives of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia there are documents from January, February, March, indicating normal command over the military police, because it is carrying out tasks for the needs of the commander of the operative zone, not for anyone else, and in that area. And, therefore, it is only normal that he should be the commander of those units." [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, do you remember having given such testimony in the Blaskic and Kordic cases?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is all in accordance with the regulations on the organisation of the military police of 26 December 1992 and I'm saying what has been transcribed, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. Nothing but what has been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying what has been transcribed, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are again overlapping to the distress of our interpreters. I'm not saying who, but it's just a problem that both must be very attentive to. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I am trying to control the way I use my time and control my cross-examination. Could my colleague please sit down and not interrupt me until I completed my sentence? I only wanted to say that if my question requires a brief answer, a yes-or-no answer, in that case the witness should answer in that way. I understand that he wants to explain certain things. He'll have the opportunity to do so. My colleague who is defending him will give him the possibility of providing explanations and additional responses. I have limited time. I put a very simple question to him, did he remember that that is what he said. I didn't ask him whether that was the case, nor did I ask him where it had been recorded. But if the witness continues to answer in this way, then I do apologise, but I have to stop him, and then there is overlapping. It would be very simple -- or much simpler if he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say that I interpret the legal provisions, nothing else. I don't depart from the law. Everything I said here was correctly transcribed on the 26th of December, 1992. That's a document I'm familiar with, and I have been testifying to that effect. In addition, I am familiar with police duties. I just mentioned what was provided for by the law, and why should it bother you if I say that the law regulated matters in this way? I haven't diminished the importance of your question, I haven't insulted you, and I didn't go off on a tangent. Why are you afraid? You say it's a document -- you say it's a certain document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Petkovic. You will be very bored, because I'm repeating something that I have said many times, and before that Mr. Karnavas has said so many times. Under cross-examination, you are held to answer, Yes, No, I don't know, I don't remember, and not to give explanations. That is what counsel is aiming at, and she is right to do so. So if you would stick to this, there would be not such a danger for overlapping, because she's trying to stop you when you want to go into explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to say that these subjects are new subjects that weren't dealt with in the examination-in-chief of General Petkovic. And in accordance with the decision that has just been taken, could that be treated as examination-in-chief and could one refrain from putting leading questions? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] These are not new subjects. I referred to the page in the transcript that resulted in a discussion in the courtroom. The witness mentioned four standard battalions. He was asked about that. Then he said that they were under Mr. Coric -- or, rather, under Mr. Stojic, the deputy head for security, except for when they were re-subordinated or attached for the purpose of combat operations. That was from the end of July 1993. In this particular case, I have the full right to inform Mr. Petkovic of what he omitted or to inform him of what he said in a different manner in other cases, and that significantly changes the meaning of his testimony in this case about the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is not in dispute. I just want to do say that these aren't subjects that were dealt with in the course of examination-in-chief, and that is the only issue that I am addressing. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I'd just like to respect certain principles. I was asked about what do I think about the fact that two generals examining each other. They have the same role, the same position, given war, so what I think about that, it is not really necessary for me to state. What is of interest here, we heard about a term for the first time yesterday, the combat part and the non-combat component of the HVO. That's the first time we heard those terms. If that hasn't been mentioned before - at least I haven't heard such terms, and these terms haven't been discussed in four years - yesterday someone mentioned those terms, and that establishes a rank for HVO units, a certain hierarchy which -- what is the combat component, what is the non-combat component. Yesterday, I couldn't sleep, because when I was the head of the military police I thought about 166 military policemen, and over 600 men were wounded while they were part of the non-combatant component of the HVO. I thought about how they suffered. I was wondering about my responsibility, how did that happen. Your Honours, could my Defence please be allowed to have sufficient time? We are not discussing useless matters here. Often such matters are discussed; that's my opinion. Time is wasted, an incredible amount of time is wasted. For years, we've been referring to counts in the indictment about the charges levelled against us. We're not defending Croatia. Some pretend that they are defending Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and I don't know whom. We're telling the truth about Croatia, about Franjo Tudjman, about the military police. We have to respond to lies. So please allow us to have the necessary conditions to deal with these matters. This is the time of our defence. It's a difficult time for us. We've been preparing for this for dozens of years now, so please allow my counsel to do her work. But if she is continually interrupted, I'd like to ask the Chamber -- well, I can see that the Chamber isn't putting many questions. You rarely put questions now. Please allow my counsel to do her work, and then everyone else can proceed. Thank you very much, but this is something I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, your counsel is doing her job. She's doing her job well. She's putting her questions, and General Petkovic will answer. There are two comments I would like to make on what you've just said. You are right. For the time being, I'm not putting any questions, and my fellow Judges are not either. As far as I'm concerned, as far as the military police is concerned, things are extremely straightforward, and this rests on the simple question: Does the military police come under the brigade or another entity? It's thanks to the questions put by your counsel and Mr. Petkovic's answer that I will be able to understand matters much more clearly. Perhaps I will even be able to understand much more clearly when Mr. Scott conducts his cross-examination. When you will call your witnesses and when -- then I hope to have an answer to this extremely straightforward question. Second comment. You said you didn't sleep all night because General Petkovic talked about non-combat and combat. When I heard that, I understood that when he says "non-combat," he means those people who are not fighting, i.e., those who are reserve people, or involved in administrative matters, in logistics, and so on and so forth. This is the way I understood what he was saying. General Petkovic is nodding, which means that that is how we are to understand this. If the military police is in combat, that means that these people are combatants. Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I think you have misunderstood me. Could you check the transcript? General Praljak's question was very specific: Is the military police part of the non-combatant component? General Petkovic said, Yes, as far as I can remember. Please check that. What General Petkovic said is perhaps the consequence of our conversation -- our private conversation last night. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given what Mr. Coric has said, it seems that Mr. Coric spoke to my client about his testimony and that General Petkovic's answers today are the result of the conversation Mr. Coric had yesterday with my client about his testimony. Could we please clarify this and take the necessary measures? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I admit that we spoke to each other yesterday. If Mr. Petkovic agrees, I can tell you exactly what we spoke about, but I think it would be better not to go into that. But if necessary, I can do so. I'd be quite happy to tell you what we spoke about. But, similarly, since we have started speaking about such matters, you shouldn't speak in the course of the break, in the middle of my Defence's cross-examination. So I'm asking the Chamber not to allow General Petkovic and his counsel to speak to each other, because those are the rules of the Court. I have remained silent about this, but I noticed this immediately. In the middle of their cross-examination, you allowed them to have contact with each other. I don't know which violation is worse, the fact that we spoke to each other yesterday or this other case. The fact that we spoke to each other about I don't know what, if someone else is guilty, are we guilty for this, well, I don't know. I'm not testifying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question about having contact with General Petkovic was quite specific and had to do with certain procedural measures or rules. I don't mind Mr. Scott being present when I speak to General Petkovic. An interpreter could assist him. I mentioned Mr. Scott because he's opposite me, but I don't mind anyone from the courtroom being with me, and I will ask General Petkovic what we should do, how we should proceed with regard to today's decision. I didn't have any contact with my client without the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, since you were on the front-line, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, as for saying that the police was the non-combatant component, well, I would like to ask the Coric Defence to say what the tasks of the military police were. And if they find that among those tasks the military police also had the task of going to the front-line and carrying out combat operations, well, then I'll withdraw everything I said. I'm not going into the fact that there were additional orders that were issued from the assistant head according to which their military police members were sent to carry out certain tasks, but that's another matter. The military police isn't defined as a combat unit, but the fact that later orders were issued and they were sent in because of certain situations, well, that fact is a different matter. So please check to see what the tasks of the military police are and see where such tasks can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, General Petkovic has explained what happened over dinner. From what I understand, he says that if the military police is on the front-line, then there is an order. If the military police is not on the front-line, then it is a non- combatant force. That's what I've understood. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, I'm receiving slips of paper from my Defence, although in certain periods I don't get any advice. I would like to read out to you from the Military Lexicon of the former Yugoslavia, and General Petkovic graduated from the military schools of that country, only a very short passage which outlines the structure of military police in all republics of the former Yugoslavia and all of its parts. I would only read out two or three sentences, and I'm quoting the Military Lexicon from 1971, which is available here in the courtroom, and this is at the same time my reply to the statements issued by Mr. Petkovic: "The units of the military police are specially-trained units for carrying out combat tasks and dedicated tasks from the purview of the military police. They are organised into squads, platoons, companies, battalions, and brigades of the military police. They are directly subordinated to the commander to whose units they belong." This is page 199 from that Military Lexicon. There is more, and this is an excerpt I took yesterday, anticipating this discussion. So this is my reply to Mr. Petkovic. And, General, do not explain here, but limit yourself to answering the questions of my Defence counsel. I know that you taught some time ago, but that's no longer the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, you weren't chief of military police in the JNA. You are -- what you said refers to the JNA. The structure that you had was different. There are two documents outlining the tasks of the military police. Later Defence counsel put that forward, and then we'll study that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, everybody agrees. Mr. Coric would like to you answer the questions put by his counsel. His counsel would like to put questions to you, and you would like to answer, so let's continue for another five minutes before the break. Please take the floor, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Well, now that I have the floor again, I would like to remind you that before this interruption, we spoke about the daily tasks of the military police and about Mr. Petkovic's testimony in the Blaskic and Kordic cases. He said that he -- he said that he remembers giving those statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I want to remind you now what a witness in this trial said about the same topic. I'm just checking whether or not the witness was protected. No, he wasn't. So it was Witness Bozo Pavlovic. The page is 46905 of the transcript, lines 6 through 11: [In English] "Q. Based on the documents we've looked at so far, it's clear that before the 30th of June, 1993, you and the commander of the 1st Brigade were issuing orders to the military police in your area of responsibility; am I correct? "A. Yes, I was issuing orders to them for the police assignments in my area of responsibility." [Interpretation] Let's now look at what the same witness said on page 46907, lines 9 through 13: [In English] "I've already said that the police in the zone carried out military police assignments pursuant to our orders, and that is precisely the job they should do, that is to say, to control the area. And anything else, if there's any crime or anything like that, then they have to prevent that." [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, do you remember this part of Mr. Pavlovic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that you have read it out accurately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It can be checked in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, it's better to read it out than for me to try to remember. Pavlovic said that he issued orders to the military police, but we don't see who gave him that right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. Stop right there. I asked you whether you remember. If you don't remember, fine. And tell me now, Mr. Petkovic, did Mr. Pavlovic confirm, by saying that, the de facto application of what you spoke about in the Blaskic and Kordic cases, and that's the same thing that I have just read out, as concerns the commanding of the military police in daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set up a link with the commander of the OZ, as far as daily tasks are concerned, and I stand by that, because those were the legal provisions. I don't know who gave the right to the lower-rank commander, Pavlovic, to use that 3rd Company of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Petkovic, all right. If you don't know, how am I supposed to know? Let's move on to document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be a good idea to have the break now, since it is nearly 10.30. During the break, Ms. Alaburic can talk to General Petkovic on the sole issue of time allocation, not about any matters of substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, before the break we saw what was in accordance with the rules, as you said, and gave your reasons, with regard to the daily tasks of the military police, and now I would like to go into the de facto situation in brief. And to do that we will look at several documents. P00781 is the first such document. Toward the beginning of today's examination, I asked you what an establishment structure was, and you provided an answer. Could you please tell me briefly what an establishment system is and whether there is a difference between an establishment structure and an establishment system, but briefly, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petkovic, you have the document in front of you. This document was signed by the commander of the Zone of Operations North-West Herzegovina, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. It's dated the 20th of November, 1992. It's called "Report on the Establishment of the Command of the OZ North-West Herzegovina," and it was sent to all brigade commanders in that area. It says here, in paragraph 2: "The establishment system of the OZ North-West Herzegovina includes the following units:" And several brigades are mentioned. And under item 9, we can read: "The 2nd Military Police Battalion - Livno." Mr. Petkovic, are you familiar with this report submitted by Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 9 is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Easy. Are you familiar with it or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that this was not forwarded to the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I follow from that, then, that your unfamiliar with it. Let's move on to the following document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General, if I did not ask any questions, Mr. Coric might be worried, but this is not the reason why I'm asking the question. I'm somewhat surprised to see the English version. It is -- we see 1 to 9, and in English it is said, handwritten, "11.05, 10.50, 10.50," and we can't find the equivalent thereof in the B/C/S version. Does this mean that there is another document? Because this is a Prosecution document. We have the number, P781, so was the translation done from another document or is there a mistake here? General Petkovic, how do you account for the fact that next to the "Herceg Stjepan Brigade," this mention would have been handwritten "11.05," or don't have you an explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this was translated from Croatian, then there should be no such tag as this handwritten "11.05," because I can see no such thing in the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a bit of a mystery. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please allow me to recall, Mr. Petkovic, you should answer, Yes, No, I don't know. You have not answered the question. You have given something which probably, and that's how counsel understood it, was meant to be an explanation. But the question was: Do you know -- did you know this document or did you not? And the answer is, Yes, or, No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question whether or not I was familiar with it was put to me later. I was reading the distribution list, to who it was forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to do the work of counsel. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I may have missed that, so it didn't enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, let's clarify. Did you answer that you were not familiar with document P00781?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my answer, and I said that it wasn't forwarded to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The following document is 5D05095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. We're going to continue, but as to the issue of answering, Yes, or, No, I don't know, I subscribe to my colleague's position. However, I do have to say that as per the Rules, nothing is said on the issue, and I want to make that clear, for it to be recorded in the transcript. In this famous Akayesu appeals judgement, paragraph 323, the Appeals Chamber says this on leading questions and cross-examination: "The Appeals Chamber --" Please listen carefully, because it's interesting: "The Appeals Chamber recalls that the Rules of the Tribunal never included any specific provision on the specific issue of leading questions. However, the Rules present general rules governing examination-in-chief and cross-examination, seemingly inspired by the US Federal Rules of Evidence. Admittedly, based on such a model, leading questions are generally authorised and used in cross-examination, whilst they are prohibited in examination-in-chief. Nevertheless, the Appeals Chamber is of the view that the Rules have their own life, once they have been adopted. The question of interpreting the Rules may be inspired by a model of domestic law it is based on, but in no case can it be subordinated to it." Therefore, the Appeals Chamber is saying here that the Rules is what matter and not domestic law, and that the Rules are silent on this, so anybody can do what they want. This is why I went along with my colleagues' position, even though I sometimes have strong reservations, because if you answer a question by saying, No, it may cause problems. But please continue. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I called document 5D05095. This is a document from the brigade commander. I repeat the document reference, 5D05095, a document of the commander of the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, dated the 21st of March, 1993. It says: "I order," and under item 2: "Reinforce manpower performing security," et cetera, and then "assign two military policemen and one civil policeman." And it also says, apart from that, "select five men for some factories." For one factory, it's the military police of the brigade; for the other factory, it's the Bruno Busic unit, and for another factory the active military police. And under item 4 it says: "The commanders of the above-mentioned units are personally responsible to me for the execution of this order." Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, does this order refer to the tasks of the military police, as you have stated it in the Blaskic case, and that is providing security to facilities.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military police's task is to provide security for certain facilities. This is part of their daily duties. This is done if it is necessary, as assessed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document, 5D04374. This is an order from the Commander of the Operative Zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina that was sent to the 3rd MP Battalion and to the Mostar Police Administration. Under item 1, it says: "Uniformed and armed persons are prohibited from entering the zone of responsibility of Mostar municipality without the prior written permission of the OZ JIH/South-Eastern Herzegovina Operations Zone ..." Mr. Petkovic, is this one of the regular tasks that the MP -- the military police have to perform, a task that concerns security and protecting the lives of people in the zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the MP's regular duties, one of their daily duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document. It is 5D04375. This is also an order from the commander of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operations Zone. It's dated the 17th of April, 1993. And it says: "In keeping with the current situation in the city of Mostar and the need to secure the city, I hereby order that the 2nd, 3rd, and 5th Battalions of the 2nd HVO Brigade and the 4th Battalion of the 3rd HVO Brigade each attach at least 50 soldiers under the command of the 3rd HVO Military Police Battalion in Mostar." And then it says: "I shall hold the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades and the commander of the 3rd HVO Military Police Battalion responsible for carrying out the order." It was forwarded to the commanders of these brigades, and we can see that at the bottom, and the Command of the 3rd Battalion of the military police. Mr. Petkovic, does this order also concern regular MP duties? We can see that it has to do with securing towns.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has to do with providing security for a town, and the army should reinforce the security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P02534 is the following document I would like to have a look at. It consists of two parts, this document consists of two parts. The first part is your order, and the second part is a document in which the commander of the operations zone in South-Eastern Herzegovina forwards your order to the relevant units. It's dated the 27th of May, 1993. It prohibits those who have to perform military service to go to the Republic of Croatia from Mostar. It says such individuals are banned from leaving the town and going to the Republic of Croatia or municipalities in Western Herzegovina, and with a view to ending such occurrences: "I hereby order:" Under 1: "All permits to leave the area of HZ-HB issued to military conscripts in Mostar shall be invalid as of this day." We can see that this was sent to the military police, amongst others. Mr. Petkovic, does this order also concern the regular duties of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This ban on leaving the town is also one of the regular daily duties that the military police has to perform. It can go on for two, three, or more days, as the commander of the operations zone will have to assess how long this shall be in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document, P04063. Again, this is one of your orders, dated the 9th of August, 1993. It has to do with bringing in deserters and those who have to perform their military service and who fail to respond to mobilisation, conscripts who fail to respond to mobilisation: "I hereby order:" And we can also see it was also sent to the Military Police Administration. It says under item 5 -- or, rather, you say: "The NVP will bring those persons in and detain them in the Ljubuski Prison, where they will be held until the end of the trial." Under item 6, you say: "The commanders of zones, brigades and units at their levels, the HVO NVP and the Military Court president will be responsible to me for carrying out this assignment." The first question I would like to put to you, Mr. Petkovic, is: What does "NVP" mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the head of the Military Police Administration, the head of the military police, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, does this document also concern the daily tasks that the military police had to perform; bringing in deserters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the military police's tasks, its regular and daily task that they have to perform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document, 3D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. As a judge, I cannot but be surprised to read that you have ordered the Military Court president to be responsible to you for carrying out an assignment. How do I have to understand this, in view of the very well-known general rule that judges must be independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, a judge is independent, but if he doesn't deal with the cases referred to him, then he has to be informed of the fact that he has to deal with referred cases. Otherwise, these cases will just accumulate and the Court will be quite useless. The date here is the 9th of August, and at the time there were many men who weren't where they should have been. They quite simply left. So the Court, in a certain sense, which is independent, has to be warned to participate in the matter and to ensure that things are done in an effective way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to discuss this. That does not mean that I quite agree with your view. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following document is 3D02584. It's another order of yours, dated the 14th of August, 1993. It has to do with -- it says leaving the zone of responsibility is forbidden: "I hereby order:" Item 3 says: "The military police shall block all exits from the zones of responsibility and prevent soldiers from leaving." Mr. Petkovic, does this order also concern the daily duties performed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police, especially within a brigade, has to block all exits from the brigade to ensure that the troops don't leave. That's a daily task, because there were individuals who would flee from the zone on a daily basis, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, one thing catches my attention. This is addressed, if I have seen it correctly, to the OZ, the operations zone, and to military police. It strikes me as so far we had gotten the impression that the military police was integrated in the OZ, and an order to the OZ would include an order to everyone under the command of the OZ, including military police. Here, it seems to be different. I wonder whether you can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's correct, the military police was in the operative zone for its daily tasks. Here it says that all exits should be blocked, the police should be encouraged to block all exits from the operative zone of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, please make sure that the microphones are closer to Mr. Petkovic. It's hard to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I may not have brought across what catches my attention. If you give an operative order to an operative zone, would you say order to the operative zone and to the artillery of the operative zone, or to the operative zone and another sub-unit of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not how this should be understood. But since the case was quite specific, well, have you this handwritten addition that says that the military police should be included, the commander of the operative zone should be reminded of the fact that he has to use the military police to block all exits from the brigade's zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it your handwriting that we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm putting my last question on this. Did you put this just for clarity, to sort of recall that this must be carried out by the military police, or is there another explanation why you thought it necessary or useful to add these words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that it was necessary so that the commander of the operative zone wouldn't say, I'll just rely on the brigade and what the brigade does. As part -- well, he also has the right to engage the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police to perform daily tasks, and then some men from the 3rd Battalion can engage individuals to carry out the blockade of the relevant exits from the zone concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'll now skip a document. We'll move on to my next subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, as an introductory step, I would first like to see what you had to say in the Blaskic case with regard to re-subordination. The number of the document is P10028. The page of the transcript is 24023; the lines, 22 to 25. Page 24024 as well, and lines 1 to 16. I'll go through that slowly now: [In English] "I mentioned subordination here, the term. When a unit is subordinated to somebody, that means that it is not within his organisation and set-up. By that reminding units of this kind and by establishing them while a situation is underway, the commander to whom a unit has been subordinated takes over all the obligations and responsibilities towards that unit, just as if it was within the composition of his own organisational entity. "Apart from not being able to do what I set out a moment ago, which mostly relates to personnel matters, such as appointments or relieving individuals of their duty, the commander of a unit which is subordinated, from that point on in time takes on all responsibilities and tasks and is responsible for them -- they are responsible exclusively to the commander to whom they are subordinated, and he is duty-bound, for all orders that he gives and instructions that he gives, to carry them out and implement them." [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, do you remember having given this testimony in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On pages 49791 to 49795 of the transcript of this case, you answered questions about the participation of the military police in combat operations, and you said that initially there was just one light assault brigade that carried out combat tasks, and that at the end of July 1993, four such battalions were established, and that on occasion the Defence Department could attach some of the standard battalions of military police for combat operations, to carry out combat tasks. You also added that towards the end of July an order was issued according to which the military police or certain elements from within the military police were to be re-subordinated in order to carry out combat operations to the HVO. Do you remember having testified in that manner? I have summarised the substance of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember having testified in that manner, and I remember all the orders I referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at what you had to say about the subject in the Kordic case, first of all, and that can be found at the following pages of the transcript of that case: 26766, lines 21 to 25, and page 26767, line 1. You said the following: [In English] "Your Honours, I said -- I said that I do not remember issuing an order just then on the 15th to subordinate the police to Blaskic. In my view, the police was subordinated through the structure of the military police and the deployment of the military police in the area of Central Bosnia. It was already subordinated to him for the execution of those tasks, so there is no need to subordinate them to him twice." [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, do you remember this statement of yours in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my very words, and I was referring to the fact that the military police was subordinated to the commander of the zone of operations, and that order -- the relevant order was still in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you said that I'm afraid of your answers, which is not the case, but my time, indeed, is strictly limited.
